metadata.title: Louisiana Leader Rubric & Evaluation Handbook
metadata.description: A comprehensive guide defining effective school leadership and leader-centered practices for Louisiana school leaders, developed in partnership with NIET.
metadata.targetAudience: School principals, assistant principals, and other school-based administrators in Louisiana

leadsSystem.name: Louisiana Educator Advancement and Development System (LEADS)
leadsSystem.overview: Louisiana's improved Educator Evaluation System builds upon and supports education initiatives across the state. The process and leadership practices supported by evaluation will be implemented through the structures of instructional leadership teams and teacher collaboration and will support the implementation of high-quality instructional materials that have been adopted across the state.
keyObjectives: Use research-based teaching and leadership standards that provide clear descriptions of practice across a range of indicators.
Provide high-quality feedback to teachers and leaders that is actionable, detailed, and timely.
Support the continuous improvement of teaching and learning using materials teachers use every day in classrooms.
Offer opportunities for teamwork and collaboration that help educators to develop their practice.
Provide differentiated follow-up coaching and support based on refinement areas.
Enable educators to reflect on their practice and share their views as part of the evaluation process.

threeProvenStrategies.name: Instructional Leadership Team (ILT)
threeProvenStrategies.description: The instructional leadership team consists of the principal, assistant principals and teacher leaders. This team is responsible for building and sustaining instructional excellence and a culture of continuous learning school-wide by analyzing student work and data, modeling lessons, leading learning, and providing feedback to teaching teams and individual teachers.

threeProvenStrategies.name: Teacher Collaboration (TC)
threeProvenStrategies.description: Teacher collaboration is a structured time for teachers to meet and collaborate with colleagues. The purpose of teacher collaboration is to analyze student work and academic data to identify what students know, can do, and need; strengthen content knowledge through practice-based learning; and create or adjust lesson plans to respond to data.

threeProvenStrategies.name: Career Pipeline (CP)
threeProvenStrategies.description: Louisiana supports high-quality induction, support, and feedback for novice teachers through career pipeline. Novice teachers receive intensive, ongoing support from mentors who have been trained on identifying needs, providing feedback, and coaching new teachers.

leadershipBeliefs: School leadership matters and has a significant impact on the quality of teaching and student learning.
Effective school leaders set high expectations for students and adults, monitor progress, and intervene when those expectations are not met.
All school leaders, regardless of their current level of performance, can improve their practice through the use of high-quality professional learning and job-embedded support.
Assessments of school leader effectiveness must be comprehensive, grounded in observed student and adult behavior, and focused on the impact of school leadership practices.
Each evaluation system component is grounded in research about effective leadership practices.

definitions.Acceleration: Just-in-time tutoring and support that strategically connects unfinished learning from prior grades or courses with new learning, rather than isolated skill practice or prerequisite review.
definitions.Expectations/Success Criteria: Concrete indicators of learning performance, such as descriptions, rubrics, or work exemplars, that make it clear to students what counts as quality work or achievement.
definitions.High-Quality Instructional Materials (HQ: Instructional content that is fully aligned to state content standards and builds content knowledge by providing a coherent sequence of content. High-quality instructional materials are often referred to as curriculum.
definitions.Instructional Leadership Team (ILT): The group of school-level leaders who guide the instructional work of the school. Members of the ILT vary across schools but often include the principal, assistant principals, master teachers, content leaders, instructional coaches, and teacher leaders.
definitions.School Leaders: Individuals in a school building who exercise instructional leadership. School leaders can include assistant principals, deans, master teachers, content leaders, instructional coaches, and teacher leaders.
definitions.Teacher Collaboration (TC): Structured time for teams of teachers to collaborate around instruction. Collaboration time is utilized in a variety of ways, including data analysis and action planning, lesson internalization, and practice-based professional learning.

rubric.name: Louisiana Leader Rubric (LLR)
rubric.overview: The Louisiana Leader Rubric was designed through a partnership between the Louisiana Department of Education (LDOE) and the National Institute for Excellence in Teaching (NIET) to directly support improvements in school leadership. By clearly defining effective leadership and leader-centered practices, this rubric provides school leaders with a roadmap for strengthening their practice, facilitating high-quality coaching, and fostering collaboration around best leadership practices.
rubric.performanceLevelGuidance: Performance definitions are provided at levels 5, 3, and 1. Evaluators can score performance at levels 2 or 4 based on evidence and their professional judgment. A rating of 2 often occurs when examination of the evidence is stronger than unsatisfactory, but there is not enough specific evidence to merit a proficient rating. A rating of 4 often occurs when many of the descriptors in the proficient level are evident and strong, but there is not enough evidence or consistency to merit an exemplary rating of 5. These ratings should always be based on close evaluation of evidence, including observations, data analysis, and stakeholder feedback.

indicatorExplanations.explanation: Effective school leaders set clear, measurable, data-driven goals and monitor progress systematically. This includes disaggregating data by student subgroups to identify and address equity gaps, using multiple data sources beyond just academic assessments, and engaging teachers in the goal-setting and monitoring process.

descriptorExplanations.dataDriverGoals: School leaders develop goals based on analysis of multiple data points. Goals are specific, measurable, and aligned to school improvement priorities. Action plans include clear steps, timelines, and responsible parties.
descriptorExplanations.disaggregation: Data is analyzed by student subgroups (students with disabilities, English Learners, economically disadvantaged, racial/ethnic groups) to identify achievement gaps and target interventions accordingly.
descriptorExplanations.varietyOfData: Leaders use both academic data (universal screening, formative assessments, interim assessments, summative assessments) and non-academic data (attendance, chronic absenteeism, discipline, surveys, family engagement metrics).
descriptorExplanations.interventionPlanning: Based on data analysis, leaders develop specific intervention plans with student-centered strategies and monitor the effectiveness of those interventions over time.
descriptorExplanations.teacherInvolvement: Teachers are active participants in analyzing data, planning interventions, and implementing strategies in their classrooms. This builds collective ownership of goals.

evidenceExamples: School improvement plan with data-driven SMART goals disaggregated by student subgroups
Action plans with specific interventions, timelines, and progress monitoring checkpoints
ILT and TC meeting agendas and notes showing data analysis protocols
Intervention tracking systems with student progress data
Teacher-created classroom action plans aligned to school goals
Data wall or dashboard displaying progress toward goals
coachingQuestions: How do you determine which data points are most critical for goal-setting?
What process do you use to disaggregate data and identify equity gaps?
How do you involve teachers in the goal-setting and monitoring process?
What systems do you have in place to track intervention effectiveness?
How frequently do you review progress toward goals, and what adjustments do you make based on that review?
How do you communicate progress toward goals with stakeholders?
What non-academic data do you collect and how does it inform your decision-making?
How do you ensure interventions are student-centered rather than program-centered?

indicatorExplanations.indicatorName: Communication of Mission, Vision, and Goals
indicatorExplanations.explanation: School leaders must establish and communicate a compelling vision that inspires and unites all stakeholders. The mission, vision, and goals should be clearly connected to instructional priorities and high-quality curriculum, creating coherence between what the school believes and what it does daily.

descriptorExplanations.establishingVision: The vision presents a compelling picture of what success looks like for the school, grounded in shared values and beliefs. It should inspire action and provide direction for decision-making.
descriptorExplanations.communicatingToStakeholders: Communication goes beyond simply sharing information—it actively fosters stakeholder investment and buy-in. Multiple communication channels and approaches are used to reach diverse stakeholders.
descriptorExplanations.alignmentToInstruction: The mission, vision, and goals are directly connected to what happens in classrooms. Instructional priorities and curriculum choices reflect and advance the school's stated beliefs.

evidenceExamples: Mission and vision statements displayed throughout the school
Communication artifacts (newsletters, social media, website) referencing mission/vision
Meeting agendas that connect activities to mission/vision/goals
Staff and family survey data on understanding and buy-in of school vision
Instructional focus documents aligned to mission and vision
New staff orientation materials emphasizing school culture and beliefs
coachingQuestions: How did you develop your school's mission and vision? Who was involved?
How do you ensure all stakeholders understand and embrace the school's vision?
What evidence do you have that teachers connect their daily work to the school's mission?
How do you communicate differently with different stakeholder groups?
How does your instructional focus align with your stated mission and vision?
How do you revisit and refresh the vision to keep it relevant and inspiring?
What would students say about your school's mission if asked?
How do new staff members learn about and internalize the school's values?

indicatorExplanations.explanation: Effective leaders advocate for all students, especially those who have been historically underserved, by establishing and modeling high expectations. descriptorExplanations.academicStandards: High expectations are operationalized through demanding academic standards that align to state standards and high-quality curriculum. These expectations are clear, consistently applied, and supported with appropriate resources.
descriptorExplanations.modelingExpectations: Leaders demonstrate expectations through their own behavior, decision-making, and priorities. They hold themselves to the same standards they set for others.

descriptorExplanations.assessmentSystems: Both formative and summative assessment systems are in place to track student progress, identify learning gaps, and inform instructional decisions and interventions.
descriptorExplanations.professionalLearning: Leaders provide ongoing professional learning focused on effective curriculum implementation. Teachers understand the curriculum deeply and can implement it with fidelity while making appropriate adaptations.
descriptorExplanations.tcAndIltStructures: Teacher Collaboration and Instructional Leadership Team structures focus on curriculum and assessment implementation. Teams analyze student work to inform professional learning and improve practice.

indicatorExplanations.explanation: Leaders develop themselves and their leadership team to effectively use the evaluation system to improve teacher practice. evaluationProcess.overview: The Louisiana Leader Evaluation Process includes beginning-of-year, middle-of-year, and end-of-year conferences between the school leader and their evaluator. Evidence is collected throughout the year through observations, data analysis, and stakeholder feedback.

components.name: Beginning-of-Year (BOY) Conference
components.purpose: Establish goals and priorities for the year based on school data and leader professional growth needs.
activities: Review school data and identify priority areas
Set measurable goals for student outcomes and leader growth
Identify evidence sources and collection methods

components.name: Middle-of-Year (MOY) Conference
components.purpose: Monitor progress toward goals, review evidence, and make adjustments as needed.
activities: Review progress data on school and leader goals
Adjust strategies and action plans as needed

components.name: End-of-Year (EOY) Conference
components.purpose: Conduct summative evaluation, reflect on the year, and plan for continued growth.
activities: Review all evidence collected throughout the year
Determine summative ratings on each indicator
Reflect on accomplishments and areas for growth
Identify priorities for the following year

evidenceCollection.overview: Evidence for leader evaluation comes from multiple sources collected throughout the year. Evaluators should gather evidence systematically and maintain documentation.
evidenceCollection.documentationGuidance: Evidence should be specific, objective, and connected to rubric indicators. Evaluators should collect evidence across all domains throughout the year rather than waiting until evaluation conferences.

scoringGuidance.overview: Evaluators determine performance levels based on the preponderance of evidence collected. Ratings should reflect consistent patterns of behavior, not isolated instances.
levelDetermination: Level 5 (Exemplary): Evidence shows the leader consistently and effectively demonstrates all descriptors. Performance is strategic and systematic.
Level 4: Evidence shows performance between Proficient and Exemplary. Many descriptors are strong, but not enough consistency for Level 5.
Level 3 (Proficient): Evidence shows the leader usually and effectively demonstrates the descriptors. This is the expected level of performance.
Level 2: Evidence shows performance between Unsatisfactory and Proficient. Stronger than Level 1 but not enough evidence for Level 3.
Level 1 (Unsatisfactory): Evidence shows the leader inconsistently and/or ineffectively demonstrates the descriptors. Significant improvement is needed.

adultLearningPrinciples.overview: The Louisiana Leader Rubric emphasizes the application of adult learning principles in professional development design and delivery. Effective leaders understand how adults learn differently from children and design learning experiences accordingly.

principles.description: Adults learn best when they are actively engaged in the learning process rather than passive recipients of information. Professional learning should include opportunities for discussion, practice, and application.
Adults bring prior knowledge and experiences to learning. Effective professional development connects new learning to what adults already know and have experienced.
Adults are self-directed learners who want control over their learning. Professional development should allow for choice and autonomy where appropriate.
Adults are motivated by learning that is linked to school goals and helps them achieve important outcomes. Professional learning should have clear connections to school improvement.
Adults want learning that is explicitly related and useful to their daily work with students. Professional development should have obvious classroom application.
Adults have existing knowledge and expertise that should be honored and leveraged. Professional learning should build on the expertise already present on campus.

researchBasis.nietFoundation: The Louisiana Leader Rubric is grounded in NIET's research-based leadership standards, which draw from 20 years of experience supporting school leaders across 21 states.
keyResearch: Leithwood, K., Louis, K.S., Anderson, S., & Wahlstrom, K. (2004). How leadership influences student learning.
Marzano, R.J., Waters, T., & McNulty, B.A. (2005). School leadership that works: From research to results.
Wallace Foundation. (2013). The school principal as leader: Guiding schools to better teaching and learning.
Grissom, J.A., Egalite, A.J., & Lindsay, C.A. (2021). How principals affect students and schools: A systematic synthesis of two decades of research.
National Policy Board for Educational Administration. (2015). Professional Standards for Educational Leaders.
researchBasis.connectionToTeacherRubric: The Louisiana Leader Rubric is designed to complement and support the Louisiana Educator Rubric. Leaders are expected to deeply understand the teacher rubric in order to provide effective feedback and coaching to teachers.
